issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: Arthur sat in the waiting room of the clinic, seventy-seven years old, his hands resting on a familiar leather delivery bag. The assault that had altered his days had occurred a few years prior, during a routine evening drop-off on his assigned route. He had been unloading a heavy crate when a customer, unsteady from a long shift, had stumbled backward and driven a heavy work boot into Arthur’s chest. The man had then kicked the van’s side door in frustration. The sharp, sudden clang had echoed through the alley, and Arthur had stood frozen, his back pressed against the cold brick wall, feeling the ground tilt beneath him. The violence had been close, unexpected, and entirely unannounced. In the weeks that followed, Arthur found himself constantly bracing. What frightened him most was the unpredictability of his own route. He was certain that a man could turn on him in any aisle, that the world had grown sharp at the edges. His beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed. He used to think that a steady route and careful attention kept danger at bay, but now he felt exposed to random force. He began to doubt himself as well. When he packed the van each morning, he would pause at the back door, wondering if he had latched it correctly, if he had loaded the heavy crates the right way. He could not trust that he will do the right thing. Arthur worked hard at keeping busy with other things. He volunteered for extra stops, organized his tool kit down to the last wrench, and spent his breaks wiping down the steering wheel. At the same time, he suppressed thoughts about the trauma. He would hum old radio tunes, watch the passing scenery, and deliberately push the memory of the heavy boot and the brick wall to the edges of his mind. He was certain that if he thought about the event, he will not be able to handle it, so he kept the door to that memory firmly closed. When the quiet grew too loud, he overated. He would eat excessively, finishing a second slice of toast or a full bag of peanuts not out of hunger but to manage the distress building in his chest. These habits settled into his days without replacing one another; they simply co-existed, filling the space he had once filled with easy certainty. The habits took root in the specifics of his daily environment. At the market, he navigated the narrow grocery aisles with his shoulders squared, avoiding eye contact with other men who moved too quickly. In his own home, his wife, Eleanor, noticed how he filled the silence with the scrape of cutlery and the turn of pages. He declined evening walks when the streetlights flickered on, and he started taking his lunch earlier so he could avoid the crowded afternoons. The consequences of these choices accumulated over months. His refusal of the later routes meant a steady drop in his weekly pay, and he began to carry the weight of it silently. At home, Eleanor noticed how he avoided the back seats of cars, how he measured his steps on the porch, as though each movement might trigger another fall. He worked hard at keeping busy, yet the busyness often felt like a careful balancing act rather than a natural rhythm. It was the morning he almost missed a scheduled stop because he was staring at the van’s side mirror, watching his own reflection, that Arthur finally decided to seek help. He had come to believe that the quiet life he was building was no longer enough to hold the fear at bay. What he hoped for most was a way to step outside without bracing for impact, a return to the predictable map he had once known. He sat in the therapist’s office now, hands resting on his knees, and spoke about the heavy boot, the brick wall, and the sudden clang that still echoed in his mind when the wind caught the alley doors. He was certain the world had changed, but he was ready to learn how to walk through it again.
